36.text: Of these calls, S˙utaˊ or Čutaˊ, Pod˙, pod˙, and Toy are of Russian origin.

37.text: S˙utaˊ (from s˙uda [сюда]) signifies “here.” Pod˙, pod˙ (подь, подь) means “Go,

38.text: go!” Toy (instead of Stoy [стой]) signifies “Stop!” Q!x! is probably an imitation

39.text: of the raven’s cry. Mra is the Chukchee word for “right.” Qu, qu; Añ, añ;

40.text: Tuˊlla, tuˊlla; — are identical with the urging calls of the Point Barrow Eskimo.

41.text: When running fast, the dogs are urged forward by whistling, shouting,

42.text: or the utterance of various short words suitable to the occasion; such as, “He

43.text: boys!” “Home, home!” “Goose!” “Reindeer!” When tired, the leader ceases

44.text: to obey the driver or to understand his calls, and accordingly looks around

46.text: The training of the leader is very simple. A swift and clever young dog,

47.text: perhaps two years old, is placed as one of the front pair in the team, and in

48.text: a couple of months begins to learn from its companion. Well-trained dogs,

49.text: when turning aside, will cast a glance towards the driver to ascertain whether

50.text: they are doing right. However, dogs that look around too often are consid-

51.text: ered to be badly trained, since this habit indicates either shyness or too much

52.text: fear, and always impedes the pace of the team.

53.text: With a strange driver, the dog-team is wayward and very shy. For

54.text: instance, if the leader knows that some turning of the road likely to be taken

55.text: by the driver is ahead of it, it will accelerate its pace to the utmost, and try

56.text: to pass before the word of command is given. A dog placed in a strange

57.text: team feels shy, and often refuses to work, allowing its trace to slacken.
